summary.query: Timing and abruptness of the Amazonian wet season onset and the dry to wet transition. Is the onset of the rainy season in Amazonia a rapid or step like transition rather than a smooth sinusoidal seasonal cycle, and how is onset date defined and detected. Observed behaviour of near surface humidity, specific humidity, dew point and vapour pressure deficit through the dry to wet transition in the western and northwestern Amazon including Loreto Peru. Changes in cloud cover, nocturnal cooling and the diurnal temperature range at wet season onset that could decouple daily minimum temperature from atmospheric moisture. Predictability and statistical model error during transition seasons compared with established wet or dry seasons. Behaviour and bias of kernel smoothing and local linear regression estimators near abrupt changes, breakpoints or regime boundaries, and the effect of bandwidth choice on bias at a discontinuity.

   - Several papers analyze the onset timing and abruptness of the Amazonian wet season, including whether the transition is rapid or gradual. For example, <paper corpusid="1666227">What controls the interannual variation of the wet season onsets over the Amazon?</paper> and <paper corpusid="4673735">Meteorological context of the onset and end of the rainy season in Central Amazonia during the GoAmazon2014/5</paper> discuss onset definitions, detection methods, and the behavior of variables such as humidity, dew point, vapour pressure deficit, cloud cover, nocturnal cooling, and diurnal temperature range.    - Papers such as <paper corpusid="55480106">On the Adaptive Nadaraya-Watson Kernel Estimator for the Discontinuity in the Presence of Jump Size</paper> and <paper corpusid="124196310">Testing for jumps in the presence of smooth changes in trends of nonstationary time series</paper> examine the behavior and bias of kernel smoothing and local linear regression estimators near abrupt changes or breakpoints, including the effect of bandwidth choice on bias at discontinuities.
